subject: Government
title: Public Corporations and Privatization
outline: Meaning and features of public corporations
Privatization and commercialization: meaning and types

modules.title: Public Corporations
modules.html:
1. Meaning and Features

A public corporation (statutory corporation or parastatal) is an organisation set up by an Act of parliament or decree, wholly or mainly owned by government, to provide essential goods and services on a commercial or quasi-commercial basis.

Features: creation by law; separate legal personality — it may sue and be sued in its own name; a governing board appointed by government; public ownership of capital; some managerial autonomy; provision of essential services; monopoly in many cases; staff who are not ordinary civil servants; accounts audited and laid before the legislature.

2. Reasons for Establishment

  1. To provide essential services that private capital cannot or will not supply.
  2. To avoid exploitation by private monopolies in utilities.
  3. To control the commanding heights of the economy.
  4. To generate revenue and employment.
  5. To promote even development across regions.
  6. To prevent foreign domination of strategic sectors.
  7. Because of the huge capital outlay required (railways, power, refineries).

3. Examples

NNPC (now NNPC Limited), NEPA/PHCN (now unbundled), Nigerian Railway Corporation, NPA, NTA, FRCN, NIPOST, CBN, NDIC, NAFDAC, JAMB, WAEC, FAAN, NCC.

4. Control

ControllerInstruments
LegislatureEnabling Act, budgetary approval, oversight committees, Public Accounts Committee, annual reports
ExecutiveAppointment and removal of board members, ministerial directives, approval of major projects
JudiciarySuits by aggrieved persons; judicial review of ultra vires acts
Public / consumersConsumer complaints, media pressure, Public Complaints Commission, regulatory agencies
AuditorsAuditor-General's reports and external audit

5. Problems

  • Political interference in appointments and pricing.
  • Corruption and mismanagement of funds.
  • Overstaffing and bloated recurrent costs.
  • Obsolete equipment and poor maintenance.
  • Inadequate capital and dependence on subventions.
  • Monopoly leading to inefficiency and poor service.
  • Conflict between commercial viability and social obligation.
  • Frequent policy changes and unstable boards.

examples.q: Why is a public corporation given separate legal personality?
examples.a: So that it can operate with commercial flexibility: it may enter contracts, own property, borrow, sue and be sued in its own name without involving the government directly. This insulates day-to-day management from the rigid civil-service procedures and financial regulations of a ministry, while government retains policy control through the enabling Act and board appointments.

examples.q: Explain the conflict between commercial viability and social obligation using electricity supply.
examples.a: A power utility is expected to break even, yet is often required to extend lines to unprofitable rural areas and to keep tariffs politically low. Revenue then fails to cover costs, maintenance is deferred, the utility depends on subventions, and service quality deteriorates. Resolving this requires either explicit subsidy for the social obligation or cost-reflective tariffs with targeted support to the poor.

modules.title: Privatization and Commercialization
modules.html:
1. Definitions

  • Privatization — the transfer of ownership, wholly or partly, of a public enterprise to private individuals or firms, usually by sale of shares or assets.
  • Commercialization — reorganising a public enterprise so that it operates on profitable, business principles while remaining in public ownership.
TypeMeaning
Full privatizationGovernment divests 100% of its equity
Partial privatizationGovernment sells part and retains a shareholding
Full commercializationEnterprise finances itself entirely from revenue, no subvention, fixes own prices
Partial commercializationEnterprise generates some revenue but still receives capital support from government

2. Nigerian Framework

The Privatisation and Commercialisation Decree No. 25 of 1988 created the Technical Committee on Privatisation and Commercialisation (TCPC) under Dr Hamza Zayyad. The Public Enterprises (Privatisation and Commercialisation) Act 1999 established the Bureau of Public Enterprises (BPE) as the implementing agency and the National Council on Privatisation (NCP), chaired by the Vice-President, as the policy organ. Major transactions have included Nigerian Telecommunications (NITEL), the cement and steel companies, NAFCON, and the unbundling and sale of PHCN successor generation and distribution companies in 2013.

3. Arguments For

  1. Improves efficiency through the profit motive and competition.
  2. Reduces the fiscal burden of subventions on government.
  3. Raises revenue from sale proceeds.
  4. Attracts foreign investment, technology and management skill.
  5. Broadens share ownership and deepens the capital market.
  6. Frees government to concentrate on regulation and core functions.
  7. Reduces political interference and corruption in commercial operations.

4. Arguments Against

  1. Mass retrenchment and unemployment.
  2. Higher prices once social pricing ends.
  3. Concentration of national assets in few wealthy or foreign hands.
  4. Sale of viable assets below value amid opaque bidding.
  5. Neglect of unprofitable rural areas.
  6. Loss of government revenue from profitable enterprises.
  7. Threat to national security and sovereignty in strategic sectors.

examples.a: PHCN was unbundled into six generation companies, eleven distribution companies and a state-owned transmission company, most of which were sold to private core investors under the BPE. Gains: private capital and metering investment, clearer commercial accountability, and an end to open-ended subvention. Shortcomings: liquidity crisis from non-cost-reflective tariffs, weak gas supply and transmission (still public), retained estimated billing, and mass staff disengagement — showing that privatization without a functioning regulator, tariff realism and complementary infrastructure yields limited improvement.

examples.q: Distinguish privatization from commercialization with an example.
examples.a: When government sold its shares in NITEL to a private consortium, ownership left the public sector — that is privatization. When the Nigerian Ports Authority was directed to run on business lines, charge economic rates and stop relying on subventions while remaining government-owned, that is commercialization.

modules.title: Types and examples in Nigeria
modules.html:
Types and examples in Nigeria is a key part of Public Corporations and Privatization (SSS 2, Government). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • Examples NNPC (now NNPC Limited), NEPA/PHCN (now unbundled), Nigerian Railway Corporation, NPA, NTA, FRCN, NIPOST, CBN, NDIC, NAFDAC, JAMB, WAEC, FAAN, NCC.
  • Nigerian Framework The Privatisation and Commercialisation Decree No.
  • Major transactions have included Nigerian Telecommunications (NITEL), the cement and steel companies, NAFCON, and the unbundling and sale of PHCN successor generation and distribution companies in 2013.
  • The Nigerian Communications Commission regulates the telecoms sector.

Worked example

Q: The agency implementing privatization in Nigeria is the:
A: BPE — The Bureau of Public Enterprises executes NCP policy.

Q: Which corporation regulates telecommunications in Nigeria?
A: NCC — The Nigerian Communications Commission regulates the telecoms sector.

examples.q: The agency implementing privatization in Nigeria is the:
examples.a: BPE — The Bureau of Public Enterprises executes NCP policy.

examples.q: Which corporation regulates telecommunications in Nigeria?
examples.a: NCC — The Nigerian Communications Commission regulates the telecoms sector.

modules.title: Revision and exam focus
modules.html:
Revise the whole topic by working through its key points in order, then test yourself with the 50-question quiz for this topic. Pay attention to definitions, differences between similar terms, and questions that ask you to apply the topic rather than only recall it.

Worked examples

Q: A public corporation is established by:
A: An Act of the legislature or decree — Statutory corporations owe their existence to an enabling law.

Q: Which is a feature of a public corporation?
A: Separate legal personality — It can sue and be sued in its own name.

Q: Transfer of ownership of a public enterprise to private hands is:
A: Privatization — Privatization changes ownership; commercialization changes only operating principles.

examples.q: A public corporation is established by:
examples.a: An Act of the legislature or decree

examples.q: Which is a feature of a public corporation?

quiz.q: A public corporation is established by:
options: An Act of the legislature or decree
quiz.solution: Statutory corporations owe their existence to an enabling law.

quiz.q: Which is a feature of a public corporation?
quiz.solution: It can sue and be sued in its own name.

quiz.q: Transfer of ownership of a public enterprise to private hands is:
quiz.solution: Privatization changes ownership; commercialization changes only operating principles.

quiz.q: The agency implementing privatization in Nigeria is the:
quiz.solution: The Bureau of Public Enterprises executes NCP policy.

quiz.q: The National Council on Privatisation is chaired by the:
quiz.solution: Under the 1999 Act the Vice-President chairs the NCP.

quiz.q: Decree No. 25 of 1988 established the:
quiz.solution: The Technical Committee on Privatisation and Commercialisation was set up in 1988.

quiz.q: A public enterprise that funds itself fully from revenue but stays government-owned is:
quiz.solution: Full commercialization means self-financing without change of ownership.

quiz.q: Which is an argument against privatization?
quiz.solution: Restructuring by private buyers usually reduces staff numbers.

quiz.q: Public corporations are controlled by the legislature mainly through:
quiz.solution: Committees, appropriations and annual reports are legislative instruments.

quiz.q: PHCN successor companies were largely sold in:
quiz.solution: The handover of generation and distribution companies took place on 1 November 2013.

quiz.q: A major reason for establishing public corporations is:
options: To provide essential services requiring huge capital
quiz.solution: Utilities like rail and power need capital beyond private reach in developing economies.

quiz.q: Overstaffing in parastatals leads to:
quiz.solution: Excess personnel raise costs and reduce funds for capital investment.

quiz.q: Which corporation regulates telecommunications in Nigeria?
quiz.solution: The Nigerian Communications Commission regulates the telecoms sector.

quiz.q: Partial privatization means government:
quiz.solution: Government divests part of its holding while retaining a stake.

quiz.q: A common cause of inefficiency in public corporations is:
quiz.solution: Politically driven appointments and pricing distort commercial management.

quiz.q: Privatization is expected to deepen the capital market by:
quiz.solution: Public offers of divested shares increase listings and retail participation.

quiz.q: ‘Privatization’ means?
options: Selling government-owned businesses to private individuals
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Selling government-owned businesses to private individuals.

quiz.q: During the struggle against colonialism, the OAU’s ‘Liberation Committee’ was based in?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Dar-es-Salaam, Tanzania.

quiz.q: ‘Commercialization’ means?
options: Giving away public services for free
Reorganizing a government agency to be self-funding/profit-oriented
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Reorganizing a government agency to be self-funding/profit-oriented.
